content: Ancient tooth proteins raise the possibility that Homo naledi, an extinct human relative, reserved a burial site for females, hinting at complex customs once thought unique to modern humans. For more than a decade, researchers have wondered why the adult fossils in South Africa’s Dinaledi Chamber look so much alike. The remains of Homo naledi , an extinct relative of modern humans, show almost none of the physical variation expected between males and females. Ancient proteins extracted from teeth found in the chamber now suggest a possible explanation: the sampled individuals may all have been female. The chamber lies within the Rising Star Cave system, where Homo naledi was discovered in 2013. The species lived between 335,000 and 241,000 years ago and possessed an unusual combination of primitive, ape-like traits and human-like features. To investigate the lack of variation, researchers from the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other international institutions recovered the first ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils. Their study, published in Cell , examined the largest extinct hominin population yet studied through protein analysis. The team used a minimally destructive acid-etching technique to extract microscopic protein fragments, called peptides, from the enamel of 23 teeth representing at least 20 individuals. They looked for Amelogenin-Y, a protein encoded by a gene on the male Y chromosome, but found no trace of the male marker. To check that the recovered proteins were genuinely ancient rather than modern contamination, a team at the University of York’s specialized chemistry facility analyzed their amino acids, the molecular building blocks of proteins. Palesa Madupe, who completed the work as part of her postdoctoral research at the University of Copenhagen, explained why tooth enamel can preserve evidence that other skeletal material may lose. “Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel – the hardest tissue in the human body – shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years. “This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it’s probably because they could have all belonged to one sex.” If the Dinaledi Chamber was a burial site reserved exclusively for females, it could represent the first known example of sex-specific burial by a species other than Homo sapiens . Such a practice could imply complex, symbolic treatment of the dead previously thought unique to modern humans, raising questions about how Homo naledi organized its society. Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York’s Department of Chemistry, said, “The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived. “These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins.” The absence of Amelogenin-Y does not, however, establish that every sampled individual was female. The researchers also identified a possible biological explanation. If the Homo naledi population was highly isolated, the gene encoding the protein could have mutated or been deleted. Males could therefore have been present in the chamber, with teeth that lacked the usual male marker. Reference: “Proteomic analysis of dental enamel from 20 Homo naledi individuals shows no male markers” by Palesa P. Madupe, Alberto J. content: Ancient DNA from cave walls offers clues to prehistoric visitors’ sex and ancestry, potentially allowing scientists to investigate who used these spaces without disturbing archaeological deposits. A cave wall can hold traces of prehistoric visitors even when it has no paintings or other visible signs of human activity. Scientists have recovered ancient human DNA from cave walls for the first time, showing that genetic material can survive on these surfaces for thousands of years. Several positive results came from unpainted areas that researchers had sampled as negative controls. The search began with an interest in the people who made prehistoric art. The interdisciplinary First Art project aims to date the earliest cave art and characterize its chemical composition. Led by researchers from Spain and Portugal, it involves institutions across those countries, the UK, China, and Germany. Collaboration with researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology extended that work to DNA analysis, taking the search for ancient genetic material beyond bones, sediments, and, more recently, bone artifacts. “We know that some of the art was applied to cave walls by blowing or rubbing pigment onto the surface. Given the enormous sensitivity of current ancient DNA analysis techniques, we were eager to see if this type of contact could leave traces of DNA in the rock art, potentially allowing us to obtain genetic profiles from the makers of the art,” says Hipólito Collado Giraldo, an archaeologist and rock art specialist from the Extremadura Government in Spain, who brought together the First Art team. The researchers examined 24 rock art panels from 11 caves, including simple marks and hand stencils, along with pigment that had naturally fallen from figurative paintings in the famous Cave of Altamira. Using advanced DNA extraction and sequencing methods, they analyzed pigmented and unpigmented cave wall fragments, sediments, bones, and a rare prehistoric bird bone airbrush used to blow red ochre onto cave walls. Of the 54 samples collected, only five yielded authentic ancient human mitochondrial DNA, genetic material found in the energy-producing structures inside cells. One came from a calcite crust with pigment underneath it on Panel 11 in Escoural Cave, Portugal. Two came from unpigmented walls in a deeper gallery of the same cave, and two others came from unpigmented surfaces beside rock art in Covarón Cave in northern Spain. The unpigmented areas had initially been sampled as negative controls, making their positive results unexpected. Two of the five samples contained no detectable mitochondrial DNA from other animals. That rare pattern strongly suggests that humans deposited the DNA directly, through saliva or other bodily fluids. The other three positive samples, all from unpigmented walls, contained both human and animal DNA. This mixture suggests an indirect route, likely involving sediment transfer or water movement carrying genetic material onto the surfaces. “Although we cannot directly connect the traces of ancient human DNA we have found to the creation of rock art, this is the first evidence for human DNA preservation on cave walls for thousands of years,” says first author Alba Bossoms Mesa, a doctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. “It is exciting to think that we may have uncovered a new way to study prehistoric human presence.” The recovered DNA nevertheless provided information about some of the people who had been in the caves. Human DNA in three samples came mostly from females, while one sample contained DNA mostly from males. The fifth remained undetermined. Further analysis of the two unpigmented samples from Covarón showed that their DNA came from modern humans, or Homo sapiens. Nuclear DNA, the genetic material housed in cell nuclei, placed them within the Western hunter-gatherer genetic cluster, consistent with findings for other ancient Iberian populations. “This study fundamentally changes how we think about where ancient DNA can be found,” says senior author Matthias Meyer, a paleogeneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology who co-led the work with Collado Giraldo. “We were surprised to see that ancient DNA can be recovered not only from pigmented samples, but also from cave walls that show no visible evidence of past human activity. We can now ask new questions: Who touched this wall? Was it a man or a woman? Which population did they belong to? How far did ancient humans venture into deep cave systems?” Sampling cave walls could offer a way to investigate prehistoric human behavior without disturbing archaeological deposits. Genetic evidence from these surfaces could help researchers establish the biological sex and ancestry of people who used caves, even where their activities left no recognizable images or objects. “This is not just about rock art,” says Collado Giraldo. “It’s about understanding how people used caves and where they left their marks.” Recovering that evidence remains difficult, even from an object expected to have been in contact with saliva. The bird bone airbrush from Altamira yielded no ancient human DNA. The most likely explanation was extremely high contamination by present-day human DNA, combined with the minimal amount of material sampled. The result highlights the difficulty of recovering ancient genetic traces from material that has been heavily handled over decades of study. Despite favorable preservation conditions at many sites, ancient DNA was detected in only one of the 24 rock art panels examined and in two additional locations adjacent to other panels. That rarity suggests pigment surfaces seldom retain enough DNA to survive for thousands of years, particularly without protection from mineral crusts or sealed environments. “The preservation of human DNA on cave walls is highly variable,” says Bossoms Mesa. “But when it does survive, it tells a powerful story. And while these first results are promising, I think our priority now should be to refine the methods and to understand under what conditions we can expect a higher success rate.” Identifying the makers of particular artworks remains a possibility for future research, rather than something this study has achieved. “This is just the beginning,” adds Meyer. “We now know that cave walls are archives of past human presence. The next step is to test more sites, art styles and techniques, especially hand stencils and figurative art in caves with good molecular preservation, as far as minimally invasive sampling allows.” Reference: “Investigating ancient human DNA preservation on cave walls and in rock art” by Alba Bossoms Mesa, Elena Essel, Louisa Jáuregui, Aurore Galtier, Elena I. title: What a day in customer service looks like — as AI changes everything
content: For Kaylee Harris, who works in customer service for a credit card company, a day at work now looks very different. Her hours used to be filled with calls, note-taking and lengthy card disclosures. Now, thanks to artificial intelligence , she can focus more on each customer, Harris told CNBC. For Shannon, AI has also changed things — but not in a good way. She works in customer service for a telecommunications company in Cardiff, Wales, and did not want to share her surname for fear of being identified by her employer. She told CNBC that AI-generated notes at her current workplace are often riddled with errors, "so I just write my own." At her previous employer, a property services company, senior management told staff to "ChatGPT it" if they didn't know the answer. AI agents booked appointments, but when they couldn't offer a customer the requested date, they passed the case to a human. Staff were "constantly fighting fires," Shannon said. "All the complicated cases came to us, causing a lot of burnout." In theory, automation in customer service should mean human agents spend less time on admin and more time helping customers with problems that require human judgment, empathy and experience. Nikola Mrkšić, CEO and co-founder of London-headquartered PolyAI, which develops voice AI systems for customer service, said contact-center agents can face "maximum abuse for minimum wage." They often deal with frustrated customers while working under strict performance metrics, sometimes without the authority or information to resolve problems, he told CNBC. He sees AI agents as a way to help shoulder that load. "It's a really, really difficult job," he said. "I think with AI, we have a shot at bridging the gap to make it better for both [customers and employees]." British telecom and media company Virgin Media O2 launched an AI voice agent in September, which it said was designed to do just that. The agent handles routine issues so human advisors can spend more time on complex or sensitive cases. At U.K.-based customer experience company ArvatoConnect, CEO Debra Maxwell told CNBC the company aims for 70% of interactions to be handled by technology and 30% by people. One AI tool it developed for the U.K. government's procurement agency, the Crown Commercial Service, generates draft supplier viability assessments with 97% accuracy, she said, reducing the need for hours of manual data extraction. As AI takes on routine tasks, human agents may be left dealing with a greater share of complicated cases — and be required to pick up the slack when the technology fails. The pressure on customer-service staff comes amid reports of rising workloads across the industry. According to MaxContact's 2025/26 U.K. Contact Centre KPI Benchmarking Insights Report , more than half of surveyed contact-center decision-makers said agent workloads had increased, up from around 40% in 2024, although the survey doesn't establish what is driving the rise. Amanda Jones, who researches organizational behavior and the future of work at King's College London, specializes in work intensification — the process by which jobs become more demanding over time. She told CNBC that AI could make call-center work even more intense if human agents are increasingly left with the toughest interactions. "Some customers may already be frustrated by the time they reach that human," she said. "One thing we sometimes overlook is that relatively straightforward tasks can provide a bit of psychological respite between more demanding ones. If those disappear, the intensity of the working day could increase considerably, even if the overall volume of work doesn't." Jones cautioned that productivity gains may also bring more intense performance targets. And as routine tasks are automated, workers could lose opportunities to develop the experience needed for more demanding work. "So, we could end up expecting people to perform more demanding work while simultaneously reducing the experiences that traditionally helped prepare them for it," she said. ArvatoConnect's Maxwell argued that average handling times may need to increase as employees take on more complex cases. "We assess whether [human] agents understood the customer's needs, exercised sound judgement and reached the right resolution," she said. "Not whether they followed a script or hit an arbitrary time target." Harris sees the upsides of AI tools, despite occasional system glitches that create more work. But she worries that the push to automate is coming, ultimately, at the expense of customer experience. "As a country, I think we are focusing on getting things done faster and choosing quantity over quality … resulting in customers being fed up with the way AI is being pushed on everyone," she said. Shannon also sees the potential benefits of using AI, but doesn't think it should ever replace real customer service. "I believe people buy from people; with AI you don't get to experience that," she said. "I go the extra mile. Can AI give that feeling? Can it feel genuine?"

final_quality.reason: The article provides a thought-provoking exploration of the impact of AI on customer service, highlighting both the benefits and drawbacks of automation. The inclusion of quotes from industry experts and specific examples from companies like Virgin Media O2 and ArvatoConnect adds depth and context, making it a worthwhile read for readers interested in the intersection of technology and human experience.
